    50: - `BUSTER_F_DECL` belongs only on header declarations; `.c`-local functions use
    51:   `BUSTER_GLOBAL_LOCAL`, and header-declared definitions carry no linkage macro.
    52: - Major files need an orientation header with ownership, entry points, and a
    53:   map using searchable symbols, not line numbers. Update it when moving code.
    54:   Name shared constants; comments explain verified constraints.
    55: - Parallel work uses the existing persistent lane gang: SPMD across threads,
    56:   SIMD within a lane, stable work-indexed results, and deterministic merges.
    57:   One-lane and `BUSTER_SINGLE_THREADED` builds use the same path. Prewarm shared
    58:   tables serially before `lane_run`; guard initialization with
    59:   `BUSTER_CHECK_SERIAL_INITIALIZATION()` and publish readiness last.
    60: - Write SIMD kernels using `<buster/lib/simd.h>` with feature/compiler guards
    61:   and correct fallbacks. Its operations are macros: arguments must have no side
    62:   effects. Design for Zen 5's 512-bit width, validate the Zen 4 tradeoff, and
    63:   preserve MSVC, AArch64, and self-hosting. Read the [SIMD guide](docs/agents/simd.md)
    64:   before changing kernels and the [parallelism guide](docs/agents/parallelism.md)
    65:   before changing concurrency or shared initialization.
    66: - New modules must be registered in CMake, added to the `ide` module list, and
    67:   included in its unity block. Wire tests into the CMake test source/header lists
    68:   and `src/buster/tests/test.c`; keep test declarations behind
    69:   `BUSTER_INCLUDE_TESTS` and private seams in `*_internal.h`.
    70: 
    71: ## Build and validation
    72: 
    73: `build.sh` / `build.ps1` bootstrap and reuse an immutable native `build.c`
    74: driver with TCC; that driver owns build policy and orchestration. CMake
    75: generates the graph and Ninja executes it. Keep workflows out of shell,
    76: PowerShell, and CMake scripting.
    77: GitHub-hosted Clang bootstrapping is a documented CI exception, not a trusted
    78: local-bootstrap substitute; see [build guidance](docs/agents/build.md).
    79: 
    80: Run from the repository root. Configure a fresh tree once, then build it:
    81: 
    82: ```sh
    83: ./build.sh generate
    84: ./build.sh build --config Release -t ide
    85: ```
    86: 
    87: **`generate` deletes and recreates its selected build directory.** Never run it
    88: alongside a build, self-host, benchmark, or harness using that directory. On an
    89: existing configured tree, use `build` for incremental work. `--sanitize`,
    90: `--fuzz`, `--lto`, `--ci`, `--time-trace`, `--instrument`, and `--cc` belong to
    91: `generate`, not `build`. On Windows use `./build.ps1` with the same arguments.
    92: 
    93: | Change or goal | Validation from the repository root |
    94: |---|---|
    95: | Before and after compiler changes | `./build.sh test_self_host --config Release` — reproduce the baseline and preserve the byte-identical fixed point. |
    96: | Production behavior | Add a focused regression, then `./build.sh build --config Release -t test_all`. |
    97: | Allocator, ABI, or backend changes | `./build.sh test_mode_matrix --config Release`; cover `none`, `mir-stack`, `fast`, and `quality` as applicable. |
    98: | Sanitized validation | With the build directory idle: `./build.sh generate --sanitize`, then `./build.sh build -t test_all`. |
    99: | Full local compiler/configuration matrix | `./build.sh test_all_combinations`. |
   100: | External compatibility work | Read the [harness index](docs/agents/compatibility.md); use its pristine pinned inputs and affected harness. |
   101: | Documentation only | Check commands against their implementation, local links, and `git diff --check`; compiler tests are unnecessary unless behavior also changes. |
   102: 
   103: Preserve Debug/Release, unity/non-unity, sanitizer/fuzz, self-host, and supported
   104: platform coverage. Test fixtures use repository-relative paths; concurrent tests
   105: honor `BUSTER_TEST_JOBS`. Report the actual revision, commands, results, and
   106: unavailable gates; never call an unrun check green. Follow the existing
   107: [rebase validation workflow](docs/agents/workflow.md) when rebasing a code change.
   108: 
   109: ## Benchmarking and diagnostics
   110: 
   111: Before performance work, read the newest audit (`tools/new_audit.py --newest`
   112: prints its path; [PERFORMANCE_AUDITS.md](PERFORMANCE_AUDITS.md) explains the
   113: history), then the relevant methods in
   114: [benchmarking.md](docs/agents/benchmarking.md). Measure using the trusted
   115: Clang-built compiler; self-built stages validate the fixed point. Compare the
   116: same inputs, flags, target, and machine. Report compile time and useful work,
   117: not just a proxy or generated-program runtime.
   118: 
   119: Record an audit with `tools/new_audit.py`: it writes one new file under
   120: `docs/performance-audits/` and nothing else. Never add a line to the closed
   121: index in `PERFORMANCE_AUDITS.md`, and never rewrite an existing audit.
   122: 
   123: ## Forge, issues, and pull requests
   124: 
   125: Use the repository/host the user names; for a GitHub URL, work on that GitHub
   126: repository. Otherwise inspect the current remote. The project also retains
   127: Forgejo workflows and a source-free GitHub runner broker; their infrastructure
   128: rules are in [workflow.md](docs/agents/workflow.md) and [testing.md](docs/agents/testing.md).
   129: Check live CI for the submitted commit instead of relying on old reports.
   130: 
   131: Historical issue references may use Forgejo numbers. Resolve those through
   132: [docs/issue-migration-map.md](docs/issue-migration-map.md) or
   133: [docs/forgejo-issue-archive.md](docs/forgejo-issue-archive.md); a current GitHub
   134: URL already identifies its issue and must not be remapped.
   135: 
   136: Write issue/PR bodies using structured arguments or a body file. Do not interpolate
   137: Markdown into shell commands. Use `--force-with-lease`, never bare `--force`,
   138: when an authorized rebase requires a force-push. Record deferred work as an
   139: actionable issue with evidence, affected symbols, validation, and completion criteria.
   140: 
   141: ## Topic references
   142: 
   143: Read only what the task touches. Detailed compatibility and frontend notes
   144: contain historical investigations as well as contracts; reproduce old results

===== DORMANT_CUSTOM_COMPILER.md =====
--- lines 1-137 ---
     1: # Dormant custom compiler reference
     2: 
     3: This document preserves the detailed architecture, testing, benchmarking, and
     4: implementation guidance for the experimental Buster-language compiler and IDE
     5: as it existed before the C-only build consolidation. Its C implementation and
     6: C test files have been removed; the `.bbb` fixtures and this documentation
     7: remain as reference material for a future redesign. None of this material is
     8: part of the current build graph, unity translation unit, test registry,
     9: benchmarks, packaging, or CI execution.
    10: 
    11: This is an archival reference, not the active agent instruction file. Follow
    12: `AGENTS.md` for current work, and reconcile this material with the current
    13: compiler before reactivating any dormant subsystem.
    14: 
    15: ## Project
    16: 
    17: **buster** is a from-scratch IDE and compiler for the buster programming
    18: language (`.bbb` files), written entirely in C with zero third-party
    19: dependencies. One executable, `ide`, contains everything: UI toolkit, GPU
    20: renderers (Vulkan/Metal/D3D12), TrueType rasterizer, compiler frontend, IR,
    21: codegen backends (x86_64, aarch64), linker, and the in-process test suite.
    22: Targets: Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS, and direct
    23: `wasm64-unknown-freestanding` core modules using Memory64.
    24: 
    25: ## Current compiler priority
    26: 
    27: Prioritize compiler throughput and producing an artifact as soon as possible.
    28: Do not add optimization passes or spend compile time improving generated code
    29: unless that work is explicitly requested. Prefer direct, predictable lowering
    30: and code generation with minimal analysis overhead.
    31: 
    32: ## Self-hosting — reproduce first
    33: 
    34: All contributors—humans and coding agents—should reproduce the current
    35: self-hosting fixed point from the repository root before changing the compiler:
    36: 
    37: ```sh
    38: ./build.sh test_self_host --config Release
    39: ```
    40: 
    41: `test_self_host` builds the trusted bootstrap compiler, compiles the complete
    42: unity-build IDE twice with buster, requires both generations to be
    43: byte-identical, and runs the stage-2 benchmark. The same build.c-owned workflow
    44: is also exposed as the `test_self_host` Ninja target. On Linux x86-64, its
    45: expanded equivalent is:
    46: 
    47: ```sh
    48: ./build.sh build --config Release -t ide
    49: build/Release/ide cc -Isrc -Ibuild/generated -DBUSTER_UNITY_BUILD=1 -DBUSTER_INCLUDE_TESTS=0 -g -v -fsource-metrics=build/ide-self.metrics src/buster/apps/ide/ide.c -o build/ide-self
    50: build/ide-self cc -Isrc -Ibuild/generated -DBUSTER_UNITY_BUILD=1 -DBUSTER_INCLUDE_TESTS=0 -g -v -fsource-metrics=build/ide-self-stage2.metrics src/buster/apps/ide/ide.c -o build/ide-self-stage2
    51: cmp build/ide-self build/ide-self-stage2
    52: build/ide-self-stage2 bench
    53: ```
    54: 
    55: On macOS, both `ide cc` invocations additionally receive the SDK returned by
    56: `xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path` through `-isysroot`, plus `-framework`
    57: arguments for AppKit, Metal, QuartzCore, and Foundation.
    58: 
    59: The target and fixed point are currently available on Linux and Windows x86-64,
    60: and on macOS. Preserve them when changing preprocessing, C semantics, IR, code
    61: generation, object writing, or linking, and report both self-hosting failures and benchmark
    62: regressions.
    63: 
    64: ## Build
    65: 
    66: Three layers: `./build.sh` bootstraps `build/build` from `build.c` using
    67: **tcc**, which then drives CMake + ninja (multi-config, outputs in
    68: `build/<Config>/`).
    69: 
    70: Keep build orchestration and policy in `build.c`, with the least practical
    71: process-launch and scripting overhead. Shell and PowerShell scripts exist only
    72: to bootstrap `build/build`; do not grow them into build systems. Use CMake only
    73: to generate/cache the platform build graph and let Ninja execute that graph;
    74: do not implement workflows, iteration, comparison, parsing, timing, or other
    75: general scripting in the CMake language when `build.c` can do the work
    76: directly. Prefer one persistent native build-driver process over chains of
    77: shell, CMake, and utility subprocesses.
    78: 
    79: ```sh
    80: ./build.sh                          # configure + build (Debug, clang)
    81: ./build.sh build -t test_all        # build and run the full test suite
    82: ./build.sh build --config Release -t test_all
    83: ./build.sh generate --sanitize && ./build.sh build -t test_all   # sanitized run
    84: ./build.sh test_all_combinations    # the full local matrix CI runs
    85: ```
    86: 
    87: `build/build` commands: `generate`, `build` (default), `clang_analyze`,
    88: `cmake_profile_summary`, `ninja_log_summary`, `time_trace_summary`,
    89: `time_trace_summary_self_test`, `test_timing_summary`,
    90: `test_timing_summary_self_test`,
    91: `import_assembly_metadata`, `test_self_host`, `test_all_combinations`,
    92: `test_all_combinations_ci`; `self_host_from_existing` is an internal
    93: build-driver worker command used only by the pooled artifact-fanout target.
    94: The combination matrix shares one multi-config build tree across Debug and
    95: Release when their configure-time policy matches. Clang's fuzz-enabled Debug
    96: sanitized and Release non-sanitized configurations use dedicated trees;
    97: dedicated trees generate only the configuration they use, while shared trees
    98: keep Debug and Release in one cross-config Ninja graph. Sanitizer rows are
    99: otherwise Clang-only. GCC and Zig cover unsanitized Debug and Release, and
   100: MSVC covers Debug and Release on Windows. Only optimized, unsanitized
   101: Clang/AppleClang builds use the requested unity build; GCC, Zig, MSVC, and
   102: every other non-Clang compiler use split translation units in Release as well
   103: as Debug. TCC is retained only as the bootstrap compiler for `build.c` and is
   104: omitted from all application/compiler combinations.
   105: The matrix configures its compiler trees in parallel, then uses
   106: `cmake/superbuild/CMakeLists.txt` for one outer `cmake --build` invocation.
   107: Each shared compiler tree builds Debug and Release through one cross-config
   108: Ninja process, so concurrent builds never write the same `.ninja_deps` or
   109: .ninja_log`. One shared CMake job pool admits the outer compiler and test
   110: commands, so a completed tree can release its slot to its tests while other

   116: unity trees use one job. Tests then run concurrently in the same bounded pool,
   117: with each tree's quota passed through `BUSTER_TEST_JOBS`; future multithreaded test work

   121: present. Trees are declared longest-first — sanitized Debug,

   123: covering two configurations, then the rest — because Ninja admits ready edges
   124: from a shared pool in declaration order and a fresh CI checkout has no

   204: ## Tests
   205: 
   206: - All tests use the `ide` executable with no external test framework.
   207:   `test_all` runs `ide test --verbose=1`, which calls `library_tests()` in
   208:   `src/buster/tests/test.c`; fuzz-capable builds then run their bounded fuzz session
   209:   in that process. Desktop CI runs the IDE window/rendering path separately as
   210:   `ide test_app --verbose=1 --ci=1`, so external Vulkan/LLVM sanitizer policy
   211:   cannot weaken unit-test or fuzz coverage. Android and iOS retain the combined
   212:   in-app test and counted graphical smoke-test flow.
   213: - Module tests live under `src/buster/tests/` as mirrored `*_test.c`/`*_test.h`
   214:   pairs. `test.c` includes their headers and owns registration. In unity builds
   215:   it also includes their implementations before the production sources; in
   216:   non-unity builds CMake compiles `test.c` and every test implementation as an
   217:   independent translation unit. Production sources expose only the narrow
   218:   seams needed by tests. Each `*_test.h` has one `BUSTER_INCLUDE_TESTS` block
   219:   around its test-only declarations and types. Each paired `*_test.c` keeps its
   220:   own header include outside one block guarding the rest of the file, so
   221:   tests-disabled non-unity builds still compile a non-empty translation unit.
   222:   Private data shared by codegen and interpreter tests belongs in their
   223:   `*_internal.h` headers under `src/buster/lib/`.
   224: - Run from the **repo root**: parser tests open `tests/*.bbb` by relative
   225:   path.
   226: - To add a language test: drop a `.bbb` file in `tests/` **and** append it to
   227:   the hardcoded `parser_file_test_cases` list in
   228:   `src/buster/lib/compiler/frontend/buster/parser.c` (covered by
   229:   `parser_file_tests()`) **and** bump `PARSER_FILE_TEST_CASE_COUNT` in
   230:   `parser.h` to match — a compile-time equality check beside the array catches
   231:   drift in every build. Valid fixtures must also be appended to
   232:   `analysis_fixture_tests` in
   233:   `src/buster/tests/compiler/frontend/buster/analysis_test.c` with their exact
   234:   semantic diagnostic count and to `ir_fixture_tests` in
   235:   `src/buster/tests/compiler/ir/ir_test.c`; this keeps the complete frontend
   236:   pipeline covered. Invalid-syntax fixtures live in `tests/errors/` and use
   237:   the parser list with exact expected diagnostics plus an expected recovered
   238:   AST expression. Commented-out entries there are known-failing/WIP.
   239: - CI (`.forgejo/workflows/ci.yml`, Forgejo not GitHub) runs
   240:   `./build.sh test_all_combinations_ci` on Linux/macOS/Windows plus
   241:   Debug+Release on an Android emulator and the iOS simulator, on every push.
   242:   Main-push CI is skipped only when the exact pushed SHA already carries current
   243:   success statuses for all four required matrix contexts; the check lives in
   244:   `.forgejo/scripts/ci_main_gate.sh` and uses Forgejo's commit-status API, so a
   245:   merge strategy other than fast-forward cannot silently land an untested tree.
   246:   The run being gated publishes its own `pending` statuses for those contexts
   247:   before the gate job starts, so the gate reads the newest *terminal* status per
   248:   context and ignores `pending`; reading the newest status of any kind only ever
   249:   sees the gate's own run and can never skip. Every other outcome — a missing
   250:   context, a non-success verdict, an API failure, or a gate job that failed
   251:   outright — runs the full matrix.

   253: ## Benchmarking and diagnostics
   254: 
   255: - **`test_self_host` is the most trustworthy and complete compiler benchmark.**
   256:   It exercises the full self-hosting IDE pipeline, including the trusted
   257:   bootstrap, two complete unity-build IDE compilations, byte-identical stage
   258:   verification, and the stage-2 benchmark. Use its end-to-end result as the
   259:   primary completeness/fixed-point signal for compiler-throughput changes.
   260:   For performance measurements, run the benchmark with the trusted
   261:   Clang-compiled `ide` executable, whose generated host code has the best
   262:   quality; buster-compiled stage executables are useful for self-hosting
   263:   validation, not as the default benchmark host.
   264: - `ide bench` (built via the `bench_all` ninja target) runs both modes over the
   265:   `parser_file_test_cases` corpus 200 times and prints one line per mode:
   266:   `BENCH_IO parse_all_tests iterations=... files=... min_ns=... median_ns=...`
   267:   reads every source during every iteration, while
   268:   `BENCH_PARSE parse_all_tests iterations=... files=... min_ns=... median_ns=...`
   269:   loads every source once and repeatedly tokenizes/parses the preloaded bytes.
   270:   Both modes share `parser_bench_run()` in
   271:   `src/buster/lib/compiler/frontend/buster/parser.c`, deliberately **not** gated
   272:   behind `BUSTER_INCLUDE_TESTS` (they are benchmarks, not tests, and must stay
   273:   buildable in Release) and deliberately independent of the windowing/rendering
   274:   path `ide test` also drives, so they run headless on a plain CI runner with no
   275:   display server.
   276: - **`BUSTER_INSTRUMENT`** (CMake option, mirrors `BUSTER_TIME_TRACE`
   277:   end-to-end — `--instrument`/`--no-instrument` on `generate`) compiles in
   278:   finer-grained bench timing, compiled out entirely by default. With it on,
   279:   `ide bench` additionally prints `BENCH_IO_PHASE`/`BENCH_PARSE_PHASE`
   280:   tokenize/parse lines (splitting `tokenize()` from `parser_parse()`) and
   281:   `BENCH_IO_FILE`/`BENCH_PARSE_FILE` lines per test file, slowest first. The
   282:   mode prefix is part of every diagnostic line so phase and per-file timings
   283:   cannot be confused between the filesystem and preloaded runs.
   284: - **`STEP_INSTRUCTIONS` lines** report instructions retired for every build step
   285:   that already reports wall time, printed straight after its `took ... seconds`
   286:   line. The one to watch is `Self-host stage 1`, which is compile throughput on
   287:   the complete unity translation unit: it is contention-immune and reproducible
   288:   to a few thousand instructions, where wall time on an idle 16-thread desktop
   289:   varies about 10% run to run. Compare it across commits — a change that only
   290:   *adds* source can regress it sharply through a latent quadratic, which is
   291:   invisible to test-time measurement. Linux-only: this needs hardware counters
   292:   and there is no cheap portable equivalent, so nothing is printed elsewhere or
   293:   when `perf_event_open` is unavailable, and its absence is never an error. One
   294:   counter covers the process tree, so a step's number is exact only while it is
   295:   the sole child running; that holds for the sequential self-host stages and
   296:   CMake generation, but concurrent matrix steps overlap and must not be read as
   297:   per-step totals.
   298: - **The `SOURCE` table** gives `STEP_INSTRUCTIONS` a denominator: it reports
   299:   what the C frontend read, in bytes, physical lines, sLOC, comments, blank
   300:   lines, literals, and preprocessing tokens, each with its share of the whole.

   307:   the files as written, `bytes scanned`/`lines scanned` what the lexer saw
   308:   after carriage returns and line splices are folded out, and two partitions
   309:   hold exactly: bytes are code plus comment plus whitespace, and lines are
   310:   code plus comment plus blank once the `both` row is subtracted. A closing
   311:   `preprocessed output` block measures the other side — the tokens actually
   312:   handed to the parser, their spelling bytes, every spelling byte the run
   313:   retained, macro expansions, and `#define` directives — because macro
   314:   expansion multiplies the input by whatever factor the macros ask for, so
   315:   parsing and lowering scale with those and not with the file sizes. The
   316:   measurement is always on and costs 0.19% of stage-1 instructions (measured
   317:   on Clang 22/Linux x86-64), because every source unit falls out of a branch
   318:   the lexer already takes rather than a second pass over the bytes, and the
   319:   output side is one linear sum over the finished token stream. The
   320:   bootstrap's table does not match the self-hosted stages' and is not meant
   321:   to: the bootstrap finds its host compiler's resource headers and the
   322:   self-hosted stages fall back to the builtin ones, which is why the file
   323:   table is populated lazily (see `map_entry` in `c.c`).
   324: - **The `SELF_HOST stage <1|2> throughput` block** is the division done: its
   325:   `workload` row reports bytes, LOC, SLOC and tokens; its `bandwidth` row
   326:   reports MB/s, LOC/s and SLOC/s from the execution time shown immediately
   327:   above it; and, where the platform exposes a hardware counter, its
   328:   `instructions` row reports the total and the per-byte, per-SLOC and per-token
   329:   ratios. These are the numbers to trend across commits, printed
   330:   by `self_host_compare_action` beside the `SELF_HOST deterministic` line. `-v`
   331:   prints the `SOURCE` table for a human;
   332:   `ide cc -fsource-metrics=<path>` writes the same measurement as
   333:   `<group>.<field>=<value>` lines for a program, each self-host stage writes
   334:   one beside its executable, and build.c combines the relevant fields with
   335:   the stage's own `STEP_INSTRUCTIONS` delta and wall time. A file rather than
   336:   another stdout line, because capturing a compile step's output would stop its
   337:   diagnostics from streaming as it runs. `bytes` is `lexed.translated_bytes`,
   338:   `loc` is `lexed.translated_lines`, and `sloc` is `lexed.code_lines`; all
   339:   three legitimately differ between the two stages for the resource-header
   340:   reason above. The LOC/s and SLOC/s values divide those line counts by the
   341:   stage's recorded wall time; MB/s uses decimal megabytes
   342:   (1,000,000 bytes). `tokens` is `preprocessed.tokens`, which does not differ,
   343:   and is the denominator to reach for when comparing the stages to each other.
   344:   The ratios carry three
   345:   decimals because a compile costs a few hundred instructions per byte, and
   346:   whole units would quantize the series to about 0.3% — coarser than the
   347:   regressions the counter exists to catch. Without a usable instruction
   348:   counter the line still prints its units and omits the ratios. Only ever add
   349:   keys to the metrics file: readers take the fields they know and must keep
   350:   working against a newer compiler's file.
   351: - **The stages' preprocessed token streams are a fixed point too**, gated
   352:   beside the executable bytes. `test_self_host` fails when the two stages
   353:   disagree on `preprocessed.tokens` or `preprocessed.bytes`, and when the
   354:   executables differ it first says whether the token streams matched — which
   355:   halves the search, since the parser and everything after it are a function
   356:   of that stream alone. Nothing else is compared between the stages: bytes,
   357:   sLOC, comments, `#define` directives and macro expansions all legitimately
   358:   differ for the resource-header reason above (currently 6.088 vs 6.087
   359:   `#define`s and 56.429 vs 56.426 expansions converging on the same 1.378.839
   360:   tokens and 12.124.867 spelling bytes). Changing what the builtin resource
   361:   headers declare can part the streams on purpose; that is the signal and not
   362:   a false alarm, because the two stages are then no longer compiling the same
   363:   program and byte-identical executables would be saying less than they
   364:   appear to. Update the gate deliberately in that case — do not weaken it to
   365:   the token count alone, since equal counts of differently spelled tokens are
   366:   still different programs.
   367: - **`ninja_log_summary <build-dir> [--limit N]`** and **`time_trace_summary
   368:   <json-path>... [--limit N]`** (both new `build/build` commands, same
   369:   shape as `cmake_profile_summary` — see `build.c`) are diagnostics for
   370:   *where compile time goes*: the former reads `<build-dir>/.ninja_log`
   371:   directly (only useful for multi-TU/Debug builds — Release is a single
   372:   unity TU); the latter parses one or more clang `-ftime-trace` JSON files
   373:   (enable via `--time-trace`) and reports the slowest `"Total *"` rollups
   374:   clang itself pre-aggregates (`Total Frontend`, `Total Backend`,
   375:   `Total InstantiateFunction`, ...), summed across every file given. These
   376:   commands are diagnostics for humans to inspect when aggregate numbers
   377:   suggest a regression, and can be run from CI or locally.
   378: - **`test_timing_summary <test-log>... [--limit N] [--baseline <path>]
   379:   [--update-baseline]`** answers *where test time goes*, the counterpart to
   380:   the two commands above. It parses the `TEST_MODULE_TIMING` lines
   381:   `library_tests()` already prints under `--verbose=1` (which every CI job
   382:   passes) out of a saved matrix run or CI log, reports each module's total
   383:   across the configurations in that run with its share of the whole, then the
   384:   slowest individual (configuration, module) rows with their deltas against a
   385:   stored baseline. `--update-baseline` records the current run.
   386:   This exists because test cost accumulates silently: `x86_64_metadata_tests`
   387:   reached 60% of all CI test CPU time before anyone noticed, and every number
   388:   needed to catch it in week one was already printed on every run and
   389:   discarded with the log.
   390:   Two properties are deliberate and should be preserved. **It is a diagnostic,
   391:   not a gate** — it has no thresholds and no CI failure condition, because
   392:   wall-clock test time is far too noisy to gate on (identical code measured
   393:   290.1 s and 319.8 s for the same matrix on an idle 16-thread desktop, a 10%
   394:   spread); recording history first is the right order, and a gate would need a
   395:   noise model that does not exist yet. **Series are per-runner and
   396:   per-configuration and are never merged** — the same module measured 4.4 s in

    21: prints every audit, newest first.** Timestamp ids sort chronologically, so past
    22: the closing id the directory itself is the index; on GitHub, the newest audit
    23: is the last timestamp-named `.md` file in
    24: [`docs/performance-audits/`](docs/performance-audits/). `--list` keeps the
    25: headlines written below for the audits the index lists and reads a later

    27: which fails a pull request that adds a line to the closed index.

    29: An audit's id is the UTC timestamp at which it is recorded,
    30: `2026-08-22T140351Z`, which is ISO 8601 with the colons dropped because Windows
    31: forbids them in filenames. `tools/new_audit.py` mints it and writes the file —
    32: mint the id rather than typing one, since it is the only field two concurrent
    33: sessions can pick identically. Seconds resolution is enough because the id is
    34: stamped when a human writes the entry, not when a benchmark iterates.
    35: 
    36: Audits up to 2026-08-22 carry the older name: a date plus a sequence letter,
    37: `2026-08-08k`. That scheme is what the timestamp replaces — the letter is
    38: chosen by counting the day's entries, so concurrent sessions reliably chose the
    39: same one. Those names are historical, entries cross-reference each other by
    40: them, and they stay as written; the two audits both dated `2026-08-02` became
    41: `2026-08-02` and `2026-08-02b` when the split gave each its own file, and no
    42: other entry text changed.
    43: 
    44: The index carries the letter ids' order, which their names cannot: they do not
    45: sort past `z` (`aa` sorts before `b`), a few entries were deliberately recorded
    46: out of id order (`2026-08-08k` says so itself), and `T` sorts before a
    47: lowercase letter, so a timestamp id lands above the same day's letter ids.
    48: Timestamp ids need no index for order, which is what lets it close.

     1: // The native build driver. build.sh/build.ps1 bootstrap this file with tcc
     2: // into an immutable, verified cache entry; from then on it owns every workflow — CMake generation,
     3: // Ninja builds, the self-hosting fixed point, the combination matrix, the
     4: // diagnostics summaries, and the metadata importers that write the
     5: // generated assembly tables. Policy lives here, not in shell or CMake
     6: // (AGENTS.md: one persistent native process over chains of subprocesses).
     7: // Commands dispatch from process_arguments near the bottom; the
     8: // build_command_names table there is the authoritative list.

   140: // --- instruction counter -------------------------------------------------
   141: // Compile throughput regresses invisibly. A change that only *adds* source can
   142: // push a latent quadratic past a threshold: `x86 metadata: decode the generated
   143: // tables once` grew the unity translation unit by ~107 lines and cost self-host
   144: // stage 1 28.8% (32.56 G -> 41.92 G instructions) through a quadratic in debug
   145: // location seeding, and nothing caught it because only test time was measured.
   146: //
   147: // Wall time is far too noisy to notice that: identical code measured 290.1 s and
   148: // 319.8 s for the same matrix on an idle 16-thread desktop. Instructions retired
   149: // is contention-immune and reproducible to a few thousand across runs, so report
   150: // it beside the existing wall-clock line for every timed step.
   151: //
   152: // Linux-only. This needs hardware counters and there is no cheap portable
   153: // equivalent; the counter simply stays closed elsewhere and nothing is printed.
   154: // `inherit` makes the counter cover processes spawned after it is enabled, and
   155: // an exited child's count is folded into this process, so reading either side of
   156: // a spawn/wait pair yields that child's instruction count without the build
   157: // driver needing to hook fork.
   158: //
   159: // One counter covers the whole process tree, so a step's delta is exact only
   160: // while it is the sole child running. That holds for the steps this exists to
   161: // watch -- the self-host stages and CMake generation are sequential -- but
   162: // concurrent steps overlap and each reported delta then includes its siblings.
   163: // Compare `Self-host stage 1` across commits; do not read the matrix rows as
   164: // per-step totals.
   165: BUSTER_GLOBAL_LOCAL int instruction_counter_descriptor = -1;
   166: 
   167: BUSTER_GLOBAL_LOCAL void instruction_counter_open(void)
   168: {
   169: #if BUSTER_LINUX

  3113: BUSTER_GLOBAL_LOCAL String8 self_host_metrics_path(Arena* arena, String8 output)
  3114: {
  3115:     return string_format_z(arena, S8("{S8}.metrics"), output);
  3116: }
  3117: 
  3118: // The self-host chain is the one place in this build where a defect stops
  3119: // looking like a failure and starts looking like nothing at all. Every run
  3120: // here is a fixed amount of work -- one compiler compiling one known
  3121: // translation unit, then the benchmark parsing the fixtures -- so a stage that
  3122: // stops progressing is not a slow machine, it is a compiler that will never
  3123: // finish. Waiting on it costs far more than the build: ninja buffers an edge's
  3124: // output until it completes, so the log says nothing at all about where the
  3125: // stage stopped, and a CI runner that serializes one job at a time stalls
  3126: // every queued job behind it until a human notices hours later.
  3127: //
  3128: // The bound is deliberately far above the work. The slowest runner in the
  3129: // matrix spends about 9 s in stage 1, 17 s in stage 2 and 1 s in the
  3130: // benchmark, and that same machine has been observed running twice as slowly
  3131: // machine-wide for hours; ten minutes is a factor of thirty over the worst
  3132: // measured stage and still fails inside the job's own budget, which is where
  3133: // the buffered output finally reaches the log.
  3134: #define SELF_HOST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 600

 15465: // --- Execution-mode matrix harness ----------------------------------------
 15466: // One gated target that cross-products the compiler's execution modes: every
 15467: // register-allocator mode (none, mir-stack, fast, quality) against every
 15468: // native object format the toolchain links from any host (x86-64 and AArch64,
 15469: // each as ELF, PE/COFF and Mach-O). test_self_host proves the FAST fixed
 15470: // point deeply but on one mode and one target; this matrix is wide instead of
 15471: // deep, so a mode/target pair whose generated code no longer works — the
 15472: // canonical argument-capture crash, the machine placement's stacked-__int128
 15473: // disagreement — fails a cheap fixture run here instead of shipping. Each leg
 15474: // links a small self-checking fixture corpus and then takes the strongest
 15475: // verification avenue the host offers: native execution when host and target
 15476: // agree, qemu-aarch64 for AArch64 ELF, wine for x86-64 PE, and otherwise an
 15477: // llvm-objdump disassembly oracle over the linked image. A leg whose avenue
 15478: // tool is missing still compiles, links, and oracle-checks; it reports its
 15479: // downgraded avenue in the MODE_MATRIX row rather than silently vanishing.
 15480: // A leg that must fail belongs in mode_matrix_expected_failures with its
 15481: // issue number — the leg is then required to fail, so both rot directions
 15482: // are caught: a regression fails the run, and a fix demands its entry back
 15483: // out in the same change.
 15484: 
 15485: #define MODE_MATRIX_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 120

 19329: // One subset, built and run a second time under LIBC_TEST_ALLOCATOR_MODE.
 19330: //
 19331: // The whole suite under all four allocators is not what this is: the compile
 19332: // alone is 33 of the run's 210 seconds and four of them would dominate the
 19333: // stage. One subset under one more allocator is about a tenth of the run and
 19334: // is real coverage -- 77 programs compiled, linked, run and compared against
 19335: // the reference's own transcripts -- where compiling the musl manifest a
 19336: // second time and counting the units that survive would have been cheaper and
 19337: // could only ever have caught a refusal, which is the half of the compiler the
 19338: // register allocator is not in.
 19339: //
 19340: // Only the test's own object is rebuilt. It links against the same
 19341: // Buster-built libc, startup object and support archive as the pass above, so
 19342: // a unit that answers differently here answers differently because of the
 19343: // allocator and not because of anything underneath it.
 19344: //
 19345: // Each unit is classified from scratch, exactly as above and against the same
 19346: // reference transcript, rather than by comparing the two Buster passes. A unit
 19347: // the reference cannot reach carries that state here too -- there is no answer
 19348: // to compare against under any allocator -- and everything else is asked the
 19349: // question again from the compile.

 39482: BUSTER_GLOBAL_LOCAL ProcessSpawnResult process_run_spawn(Arena* arena, ProcessRun* run)
 39483: {
 39484:     if (run->flags & PROCESS_RUN_FLAG_PRINT_COMMAND)
 39485:     {
 39486:         command_print(run->arguments);
 39487:     }
 39488: 
 39489:     bool restore_directory = false;
 39490: #if BUSTER_WINDOWS
 39491:     char16 old_directory_buffer[BUSTER_KB(32) / sizeof(char16)];
 39492:     DWORD old_directory_length = 0;
 39493:     if (run->working_directory.pointer && run->working_directory.length)
 39494:     {
 39495:         old_directory_length = GetCurrentDirectoryW(BUSTER_ARRAY_LENGTH(old_directory_buffer), old_directory_buffer);
 39496:         if (old_directory_length > 0 && old_directory_length < BUSTER_ARRAY_LENGTH(old_directory_buffer))
 39497:         {
 39498:             TemporalArena temp = scratch_begin(&arena, 1);
 39499:             String16 directory16 = string16_from_string8(temp.arena, run->working_directory, true);
 39500:             restore_directory = SetCurrentDirectoryW(directory16.pointer) != 0;
 39501:             scratch_end(temp);
 39502:         }
 39503:     }

===== docs/a64-darwin-relocation-closure.md =====
--- lines 3-52 ---
     3: This tranche owns the object, native-link, and JIT relocation boundary.  The
     4: exact AArch64 object-relocation denominator is the 12 enum members below
     5: (common `ABS64` is listed separately because it is shared by both targets):
     6: 
     7: `CALL26`, `JUMP26`, `PREL32`, `MACH_PAGE21`, `MACH_PAGEOFF12`,
     8: `MACH_TLVP_PAGE21`, `MACH_TLVP_PAGEOFF12`, `PE_TLS_INDEX_ADRP`,
     9: `PE_TLS_INDEX_LO12`, `PE_TLS_OFFSET12`, `TLSLE_ADD_TPREL_HI12`, and
    10: `TLSLE_ADD_TPREL_LO12`.
    11: 
    12: | Path | Supported | Explicitly excluded |
    13: | --- | --- | --- |
    14: | Mach-O writer/reader | `CALL26/JUMP26`, `PREL32`, `ABS64`, `PAGE21/PAGEOFF12`, `TLVP PAGE21/PAGEOFF12` | TLSLE/PE TLS are non-Mach-O formats |
    15: | `object_link_executable` | `CALL26/JUMP26`, `PREL32`, `ABS64`, `PAGE21/PAGEOFF12` | TLVP and all TLS forms (`OBJECT_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_TARGET`); no platform resolver exists in a standalone mapping |
    16: | JIT | `ABS64`, native `PC32`, `CALL26/JUMP26`, `PREL32`, `PAGE21/PAGEOFF12`; bound external data is accepted for direct page/absolute relocations | TLVP and all TLS forms (`JIT_ERROR_TLS_UNSUPPORTED`); unresolved external data without a binding remains `JIT_ERROR_EXTERNAL_DATA` |
    17: | Native Darwin link | local `CALL26/JUMP26`, `PREL32`, `ABS64`, `PAGE21/PAGEOFF12`, and TLVP descriptor forms | external TLVP without a local descriptor/resolver and TLSLE; out-of-range branches return `LINK_ERROR_RELOCATION` because this layout has no safe insertion point for a veneer pool |
    18: 
    19: Mach-O relocation type numbers remain unchanged: `2` branch/call, `3`
    20: `PAGE21`, `4` `PAGEOFF12`, `8` TLVP `PAGE21`, and `9` TLVP `PAGEOFF12`.
    21: Scattered addend records are accepted for all five page/branch families,
    22: including TLVP, and malformed instruction shapes, alignment, scale, and
    23: checked addend overflow fail before a patch is committed.
    24: 
    25: Mach-O arm64 `PREL32` is represented by the canonical `SUBTRACTOR`/`UNSIGNED`
    26: pair. Its source offset and section layout must be 4-byte aligned and its
    27: stored signed addend must fit `int32_t`; the writer rewrites the relocated word
    28: even when that addend is zero. A bare arm64 32-bit `UNSIGNED` record is rejected
    29: for regular sections (debug `ABS32` remains supported). Callers that construct
    30: `ObjectFile` values directly still need valid section and symbol indexes;
    31: writer, in-memory linker, and JIT preflight reject malformed PREL32
    32: alignment/range inputs, while serialized readers check section-base arithmetic
    33: before mapping relocations.
    34: 
    35: ## Verification snapshot
    36: 
    37: On the Linux x86-64 host with Clang 22.1.8:
    38: 
    39: | Configuration | Full assertions | Object | JIT | Link |
    40: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    41: | Debug | 272,520 | 541 | 114 | 314 |
    42: | Release | 272,520 | 541 | 114 | 314 |
    43: | ASAN/UBSAN | 270,936 | 538 | 98 | 272 |
    44: 
    45: The three owned production translation units also pass strict GCC, Clang, and
    46: Zig C17 syntax compilation. The checked-in A64 canonical source snapshot used by
    47: the surrounding M1 work is SHA-256
    48: `8485c5c61835d5394d325757ab2964890e8bdfea304c6faa8fd4c23e4c7aabec`.
    49: 
    50: LLVM 22.1.8's `llvm-mc -triple arm64-apple-macos` emitted the canonical
    51: `SUBTRACTOR`/`UNSIGNED` PREL32 pair, and the Buster Darwin linker accepted that
    52: object. The Release `test_self_host` fixed-point and benchmark gate also pass.
===== docs/aarch64-atomic-pair-validation.md =====
--- lines 1-94 ---
     1: # AArch64 wide atomic update validation
     2: 
     3: This is the test contract for the RMW/CAS continuation of #36 after #453, not
     4: permission to retire the direct backend. Current run results belong in a new
     5: immutable performance audit and the implementation PR.
     6: 
     7: ## Selected sequence
     8: 
     9: `MACHINE_A64_ATOMIC_RMW_PAIR` and `MACHINE_A64_ATOMIC_CAS_PAIR` operate on
    10: sixteen-byte integer frame values. Existing canonical lowering supplies promoted
    11: aggregate images. The constrained address is X10; observed halves are X9/X14,
    12: operand halves are X11/X12, and the store-exclusive status is W13. CAS stages
    13: its desired halves in X15/X17. X16 remains frame-address scratch. Metadata
    14: publishes every clobber and flags definition, plus read/write and barrier effects.
    15: 
    16: Each retry loads frame operands before LDXP/LDAXP. Only register operations
    17: occur between that load-exclusive and STXP/STLXP; there are no frame reloads,
    18: ordinary loads/stores, or calls in the exclusive window. RMW arithmetic carries
    19: or borrows across both limbs. CAS compares both halves and selects either the
    20: desired value or the observed value for the store. Even a mismatch must complete
    21: a successful store-exclusive before returning the observed pair: an unvalidated
    22: pair-exclusive load need not be single-copy atomic. The direct oracle follows
    23: the same atomicity and progress rules. Stronger ordering on a failed comparison
    24: is permitted; unsupported memory orders are not invented by the selector.
    25: 
    26: The architecture issue underlying the failed-CAS repair is also documented by
    27: [GCC PR111404's AArch64 correction](https://gcc.gnu.org/pipermail/gcc-cvs/2023-November/394322.html).
    28: 
    29: ## Permanent tests
    30: 
    31: - `machine_test_a64_atomic_pair_updates` exercises both frontend forms, six RMW
    32:   operations plus strong/weak CAS, and six valid ordering combinations. It
    33:   checks payload validation, constrained registers, small/large frame expansion,
    34:   retry destinations, and the absence of unrelated memory accesses in an
    35:   exclusive window. `tests/aarch64_atomic_update_pair_oracle.s` retains an
    36:   independent mnemonic assembly reference.
    37: - `tests/basic_c_aarch64_atomic_update_pair.c` uses a two-u64-limb arithmetic
    38:   reference. Its ten Buster functions cover all bit positions, mixed limbs,
    39:   returned-old values, carry/borrow, strong/weak CAS, signed atomic wrap, a large
    40:   frame, a padding-free aggregate and the original promoted nine-byte aggregate.
    41:   The driver requires ten functions and zero fallback across three AArch64
    42:   desktop targets, four allocators and both frontend forms; matching native
    43:   hosts execute the result. Existing aggregate and i128 census inputs also
    44:   require zero fallback and are not reduced.
    45: - `compiler_driver_test_atomic_pair_contention` is registered on native Linux
    46:   and macOS AArch64 hosts with a configured external compiler. Two independent
    47:   all-host controls precede eight Buster/host combinations (four allocators,
    48:   two frontend forms). The subject's six pointer/scalar-signature functions must
    49:   have zero fallback. The host owns pthreads, independent atomic operations,
    50:   ticket accounting and a thirty-second alarm; a parent deadline also bounds
    51:   execution. Tests cover lost/duplicate updates through a low-limb carry,
    52:   complement-pair tearing on failed CAS, both directions of acquire/release
    53:   publication of ordinary payload fields, and sequentially consistent
    54:   store-buffering outcomes. Stress is supplementary evidence, not an exhaustive
    55:   proof of the memory model.
    56: 
    57: ## External aggregate oracle boundary
    58: 
    59: The promoted nine-byte representation and deterministic zero padding are Buster
    60: contracts. Keep their original source and assertions under `__BUSTER__`; they
    61: still run in every Buster mode and remain included in the exact ten-function
    62: count. External Clang controls instead exercise the added padding-free Pair
    63: aggregate and all portable integer/ordering cases. Do not claim external
    64: agreement about unspecified promoted padding or apply a larger representation's
    65: comparison rules to a smaller non-atomic expected object. The initial external
    66: Clang run of the promoted case failed; retain it as a failed oracle attempt,
    67: not a passing comparison or a Buster regression.
    68: 
    69: ## Reproduction
    70: 
    71: Use the ordinary repository build driver and an idle configured build directory:
    72: 
    73: ```sh
    74: ./build.sh build --config Release -t test_all
    75: ./build.sh test_self_host --config Release
    76: ./build.sh test_mode_matrix --config Release
    77: ```
    78: 
    79: On an AArch64 Linux host, independent native controls can additionally run:
    80: 
    81: ```sh
    82: clang -std=gnu11 -O2 -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing -funsigned-char \
    83:   tests/basic_c_aarch64_atomic_update_pair.c -latomic -o /tmp/pair-reference
    84: /tmp/pair-reference
    85: clang -std=gnu11 -O2 -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing -funsigned-char -pthread \
    86:   tests/host_atomic_pair_contention.c tests/basic_c_atomic_pair_contention.c \
    87:   -latomic -o /tmp/pair-contention
    88: /tmp/pair-contention
    89: ```
    90: 
    91: Repeat the contention control with GCC and both controls at O0. Host compiler,
    92: source revision, native architecture, sanitizer configuration and actual test
    93: results must accompany acceptance. Foreign object generation alone is not
    94: native execution; a clean stress run alone is not performance acceptance.

    73: - **`STEP_INSTRUCTIONS` lines** report instructions retired for every build step
    74:   that already reports wall time, printed straight after its `took ... seconds`

    84:   the sole child running; that holds for the sequential self-host stages and
    85:   CMake generation, but concurrent matrix steps overlap and must not be read as
    86:   per-step totals.
    87: - **The `SOURCE` table** gives `STEP_INSTRUCTIONS` a denominator: it reports
    88:   what the C frontend read, in bytes, physical lines, sLOC, comments, blank
    89:   lines, literals, and preprocessing tokens, each with its share of the whole.
    90:   `ide cc -v` prints it, and the self-host stages pass `-v` so it lands in the
    91:   log beside their instruction counts. The `unique` column covers the distinct
    92:   files of the include closure, the `lexed` column every inclusion: a header
    93:   with neither `#pragma once` nor a whole-file `#ifndef` include guard the
    94:   preprocessor recognizes (see `CIncludeGuardTable` in `c_source.c`) is
    95:   re-read and re-lexed at each `#include`, so the two columns' ratio is the
    96:   unit's include amplification (currently 295 files/27,2 MB against
    97:   326/27,3 MB; before the guard optimization the same tree read 448/29,4 MB).
    98:   A `files lexed more than once` block under the table attributes the
    99:   remainder per path — deliberately re-includable files like the builtin
   100:   `stddef.h` and glibc's `bits/wordsize.h`, whose re-reads total 28 KB. `bytes on disk`/`physical lines` measure
   101:   the files as written, `bytes scanned`/`lines scanned` what the lexer saw
   102:   after carriage returns and line splices are folded out, and two partitions
   103:   hold exactly: bytes are code plus comment plus whitespace, and lines are
   104:   code plus comment plus blank once the `both` row is subtracted. A closing
   105:   `preprocessed output` block measures the other side — the tokens actually
   106:   handed to the parser, their spelling bytes, every spelling byte the run
   107:   retained, macro expansions, and `#define` directives — because macro
   108:   expansion multiplies the input by whatever factor the macros ask for, so
   109:   parsing and lowering scale with those and not with the file sizes. The
   110:   measurement is always on and costs 0.19% of stage-1 instructions (measured
   111:   on Clang 22/Linux x86-64), because every source unit falls out of a branch
   112:   the lexer already takes rather than a second pass over the bytes, and the
   113:   output side is one linear sum over the finished token stream. The
   114:   bootstrap's table does not match the self-hosted stages' and is not meant
   115:   to: the bootstrap finds its host compiler's resource headers and the
   116:   self-hosted stages fall back to the builtin ones, which is why the file
   117:   table is populated lazily (see `map_entry` in `c_source.c`).
   118: - **The `SELF_HOST stage <1|2> throughput` block** is the division done: its
   119:   `workload` row reports bytes, LOC, SLOC and tokens; its `bandwidth` row
   120:   reports MB/s, LOC/s and SLOC/s from the execution time shown immediately
   121:   above it; and, where the platform exposes a hardware counter, its
   122:   `instructions` row reports the total and the per-byte, per-SLOC and per-token
   123:   ratios. These are the numbers to trend across commits, printed
   124:   by `self_host_compare_action` beside the `SELF_HOST fixed_point` line. `-v`
   125:   prints the `SOURCE` table for a human;
   126:   `ide cc -fsource-metrics=<path>` writes the same measurement as
   127:   `<group>.<field>=<value>` lines for a program, each self-host stage writes
   128:   one beside its executable, and build.c combines the relevant fields with
   129:   the stage's own `STEP_INSTRUCTIONS` delta and wall time. A file rather than
   130:   another stdout line, because capturing a compile step's output would stop its
   131:   diagnostics from streaming as it runs. `bytes` is `lexed.translated_bytes`,
   132:   `loc` is `lexed.translated_lines`, and `sloc` is `lexed.code_lines`; all
   133:   three legitimately differ between the two stages for the resource-header
   134:   reason above. The LOC/s and SLOC/s values divide those line counts by the
   135:   stage's recorded wall time; MB/s uses decimal megabytes
   136:   (1,000,000 bytes). `tokens` is `preprocessed.tokens`, which does not differ,
   137:   and is the denominator to reach for when comparing the stages to each other.
   138:   The ratios carry three
   139:   decimals because a compile costs a few hundred instructions per byte, and
   140:   whole units would quantize the series to about 0.3% — coarser than the
   141:   regressions the counter exists to catch. Without a usable instruction
   142:   counter the line still prints its units and omits the ratios. Only ever add
   143:   keys to the metrics file: readers take the fields they know and must keep
   144:   working against a newer compiler's file.
   145: - **The stages' preprocessed token streams are a fixed point too**, gated
   146:   beside the executable bytes. `test_self_host` fails when the two stages

   148:   executables differ it first says whether the token streams matched — which
   149:   halves the search, since the parser and everything after it are a function
   150:   of that stream alone. Nothing else is compared between the stages: bytes,
   151:   sLOC, comments, `#define` directives and macro expansions all legitimately
   152:   differ for the resource-header reason above (currently 6.088 vs 6.087

   155:   headers declare can part the streams on purpose; that is the signal and not
   156:   a false alarm, because the two stages are then no longer compiling the same
   157:   program and byte-identical executables would be saying less than they

   159:   the token count alone, since equal counts of differently spelled tokens are

   332:   ./build.sh generate --sanitize && ./build.sh build -t ide

   346:     the runtime ahead of any inherited `LD_PRELOAD` for its own test targets;
   347:     only ad-hoc command lines need the `LD_PRELOAD=` prefix.
   348:   - **Run on a quiet machine.** A contended host produces the same visual

   350:     scheduler. Confirm the sample count and the `TEST_MODULE_TIMING` line agree
   351:     with a serial run before reading anything into the histogram.

     1: # Build and self-hosting
     2: 
     3: [Agent instructions](../../AGENTS.md) · Paths and commands below are relative to the repository root.
     4: 
     5: **`generate` deletes and recreates its selected build directory** (`build/`
     6: by default). Finish any build, test, or compatibility-harness run using that
     7: directory before regenerating it; otherwise the running compiler and its
     8: outputs can disappear and be reported as compiler failures. Reuse the
     9: configured tree with `build` for ordinary rebuilds.
    10: 
    11: ## Self-hosting — reproduce first
    12: 
    13: All contributors—humans and coding agents—should reproduce the current
    14: self-hosting fixed point from the repository root before changing the compiler:
    15: 
    16: ```sh
    17: ./build.sh test_self_host --config Release
    18: ```
    19: 
    20: `test_self_host` builds the trusted bootstrap compiler, compiles the complete
    21: unity-build compiler executable twice with its own C compiler, requires both
    22: generations to be byte-identical, and runs the stage-2 benchmark. The same build.c-owned workflow
    23: is also exposed as the `test_self_host` Ninja target. The build-driver command
    24: configures a missing build tree automatically. On Linux x86-64, its expanded
    25: equivalent below assumes a configured tree; on a fresh checkout, first run
    26: `./build.sh generate`:
    27: 
    28: ```sh
    29: ./build.sh build --config Release -t ide
    30: build/Release/ide cc -Isrc -Ibuild/generated -DBUSTER_UNITY_BUILD=1 -DBUSTER_INCLUDE_TESTS=0 -g -v -fsource-metrics=build/ide-self.metrics src/buster/apps/ide/ide.c -lm -o build/ide-self
    31: build/ide-self cc -Isrc -Ibuild/generated -DBUSTER_UNITY_BUILD=1 -DBUSTER_INCLUDE_TESTS=0 -g -v -fsource-metrics=build/ide-self-stage2.metrics src/buster/apps/ide/ide.c -lm -o build/ide-self-stage2
    32: cmp build/ide-self build/ide-self-stage2
    33: build/ide-self-stage2 bench
    34: ```
    35: 
    36: On macOS, both `ide cc` invocations additionally receive the SDK returned by
    37: `xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path` through `-isysroot`, plus `-framework`
    38: arguments for AppKit, Metal, QuartzCore, and Foundation.
    39: 
    40: The target and fixed point are currently available on Linux and Windows x86-64,
    41: and on macOS. Preserve them when changing preprocessing, C semantics, IR, code
    42: generation, object writing, or linking, and report both self-hosting failures and benchmark
    43: regressions.
    44: 
    45: The stronger Linux x86-64 gate is `./build.sh test_self_host_audit --config Release`
    46: (on an already configured tree). It repeats three generations, compares token,
    47: IR, MIR, diagnostic and binary evidence, and checks every child in all four
    48: allocator modes before reuse. `./build.sh self_host_audit_self_test` exercises
    49: the checker without building the compiler. See [the invariant and evidence
    50: contract](../self-host-audit.md); this does not replace the ordinary gate.
    51: 
    52: ## Build
    53: 
    54: Three layers: `./build.sh` / `./build.ps1` bootstrap `build.c` using **tcc**,
    55: then the native driver runs CMake + ninja (multi-config, outputs in
    56: `build/<Config>/`). The wrappers retain immutable drivers under
    57: `.cache/bootstrap-driver/`, outside generated build trees. A warm invocation
    58: reuses an entry only after validating its compiler-and-flags key, complete TCC
    59: dependency closure and executable SHA-256. Cold concurrent invocations publish
    60: unique executable names and complete markers, so no process replaces a driver
    61: another process is constructing or executing. Failed or interrupted entries
    62: lack a valid marker and are ignored.
    63: 
    64: The GitHub-hosted workflows are the bootstrap exception: the supplementary
    65: privacy broker and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` both compile `build.c` with the
    66: Clang already on the hosted image, because those images ship no TCC and modern
    67: macOS cannot run it, and because the broker must not download an unpinned
    68: compiler before it receives source. Neither produces a trusted or reusable
    69: compiler artifact. The broker also does not run the multi-compiler combination
    70: matrix, because it installs nothing; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` does, after
    71: installing a pinned and checksummed Zig and the distribution's mold, both of
    72: which the images lack. Canonical local and Forgejo workflows continue to
    73: bootstrap with TCC.
    74: 
    75: On Linux, distribution TCC 0.9.27 can reject inferred-size arrays containing
    76: compound literals in shared `string.c`/`os.c` before the driver runs. TinyCC
    77: `0fb54300b56512754221d80adda85ddb9815bceb` (0.9.28rc) bootstraps this tree
    78: without changing those initializers. Keep the chosen TCC source/binary identity
    79: with local validation evidence; the older compiler's failure is not a reason
    80: to report a Clang-built driver as the canonical TCC bootstrap.
    81: 
    82: Keep build orchestration and policy in `build.c`, with the least practical
    83: process-launch and scripting overhead. Shell and PowerShell scripts exist only
    84: to select or bootstrap the cached driver; do not grow them into build systems. Use CMake only
    85: to generate/cache the platform build graph and let Ninja execute that graph;
    86: do not implement workflows, iteration, comparison, parsing, timing, or other
    87: general scripting in the CMake language when `build.c` can do the work
    88: directly. Prefer one persistent native build-driver process over chains of
    89: shell, CMake, and utility subprocesses.
    90: 
    91: ```sh
    92: ./build.sh generate                 # configure a fresh tree (Debug, clang)
    93: ./build.sh                          # build the configured tree (Debug by default)
    94: ./build.sh build -t test_all        # build and run the full test suite
    95: ./build.sh build --config Release -t test_all
    96: ./build.sh generate --sanitize && ./build.sh build -t test_all   # sanitized run
    97: ./build.sh test_all_combinations    # the full local matrix CI runs
    98: ```
    99: 
   100: Build-driver commands (normally invoked through `build.sh` / `build.ps1`): `bench_throughput`, `bench_throughput_ci`, `generate`, `build` (default), `clang_analyze`, `test_cjson`, `test_zlib`, `test_lua`, `test_yyjson`, `test_stb`, `test_lz4`, `test_sqlite`, `test_sbase`, `test_doom`, `test_quickjs`, `test_musl`, `test_cpython`,
   101: `cmake_profile_summary`, `ninja_log_summary`, `time_trace_summary`,

   113: `native_retirement_census` freezes the tracked C regression inputs and the full
   114: native target/allocator/frontend/PIC object matrix before running any selected
   115: groups. It supports an independently pinned direct compiler, fixture/target
   116: filters and deterministic shards without removing unexecuted rows from its
   117: manifest. Executed rows require the reviewed SHA-256 support contract and an
   118: explicit resource-header directory; both compiler legs use its frozen copy with
   119: a replacement environment and no implicit system includes. See the
   120: [census contract](../native-retirement-census.md) for retained evidence, strict
   121: failure accounting and its explicit object/per-function limits.
   122: 
   123: `generate --cc gcc` and the GCC combination row share native discovery policy:
   124: macOS selects `gcc-15` from PATH (Homebrew GCC 15); other platforms select `gcc`.
   125: Set `BUSTER_GCC` to a name or executable path to choose another installed GCC.
   126: The driver probes the C preprocessor identity, rejecting Clang even though it
   127: defines `__GNUC__`, and prints the resolved executable, identity, target triple
   128: and complete version before any tree is removed or configured. A missing or
   129: unusable compiler fails; there is no fallback to Apple's unversioned shim.
   130: For this named GCC row, use `BUSTER_GCC` instead of a conflicting
   131: `-DCMAKE_C_COMPILER` passthrough override. Other `--cc` selections keep their
   132: existing behavior.
   133: 
   134: `compiler_discovery_self_test` runs before both combination matrices. It checks
   135: platform/override selection and identity parsing, exercises the real Clang
   136: preprocessor, and launches negative `generate --cc gcc` children with Clang,
   137: a missing executable and a conflicting CMake override. Each must report the
   138: specific failure and preserve an existing configuration sentinel. macOS also reports the actual unversioned
   139: `gcc` identity, independently of the selected versioned GCC row.
   140: 
   141: `musl_directory_self_test` checks complete, unique directory inventories through
   142: two capacity growths, opposite creation orders, manifest sorting and architecture
   143: replacement, empty/error paths, and symbolic-link refusal. It runs before the
   144: local and CI combination matrices on Windows and POSIX; Windows reports when
   145: the host lacks permission to create the test link.
   146: 
   147: `test_mode_matrix` (`./build.sh test_mode_matrix --config Release`, also a
   148: Ninja target) is the execution-mode cross product: every register-allocator
   149: mode (`none`, `mir-stack`, `fast`, `quality`) against every native target the
   150: toolchain cross-links from any host — x86-64 and AArch64, each as ELF, PE and
   151: Mach-O, 24 legs. Where `test_self_host` is deep on one mode and one target,
   152: this matrix is wide: each leg links a small self-checking fixture corpus
   153: (`basic_c_call_abi`, `basic_c_x86_64_i128_stack_abi`, `basic_c_float_abi`,
   154: `basic_c_vector_register_pressure`) at the default CPU model and then takes
   155: the strongest verification avenue the host offers — native execution when
   156: host and target agree, `qemu-aarch64` for AArch64 ELF, `wine` for x86-64 PE,
   157: and an `llvm-objdump` disassembly oracle for images nothing on the host can
   158: run. A leg whose avenue tool is missing still compiles, links and
   159: oracle-checks, and reports the downgraded avenue in its `MODE_MATRIX` row
   160: rather than vanishing. A leg that must fail belongs in
   161: `mode_matrix_expected_failures` in `build.c` with its issue number; the leg
   162: is then required to fail, so a regression and a silently landed fix are both
   163: caught. Fixture runs are deliberately uncaptured — wine's background services
   164: inherit captured pipe ends and stretch a 10 ms run to seconds — and every
   165: child is bounded by `MODE_MATRIX_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`. The whole matrix costs
   166: about four seconds on a warm tree; CI runs it on the dedicated Linux runner
   167: and on macOS (where the Mach-O rows execute natively), and skips the Windows
   168: runner because that box is the CI wall-time gate and its PE rows already run
   169: under wine on Linux. GitHub CI runs it on all four of its Unix runners, which
   170: is what makes the ELF and Mach-O rows execute natively at both x86-64 and
   171: AArch64; those images carry no wine, so their PE rows stay on the oracle.
   172: The combination matrix shares one multi-config build tree across configurations
   173: when their configure-time policy matches. Clang omits unsanitized Debug because
   174: sanitized Debug provides the stronger coverage; it builds and runs unsanitized
   175: Release plus sanitized Debug and Release. Non-Apple Clang configurations use
   176: dedicated trees because their fuzz-runtime policy differs, while AppleClang's
   177: two sanitized configurations share one cross-config Ninja graph. GCC and Zig
   178: compile unsanitized Debug only and do not execute it; MSVC does the same on
   179: Windows. Only optimized, unsanitized Clang/AppleClang builds use the requested
   180: unity build; every other build uses split translation units. TCC is retained
   181: only as the bootstrap compiler for `build.c` and is omitted from all
   182: application/compiler combinations.
   183: The matrix configures its compiler trees in parallel, then uses
   184: `cmake/superbuild/CMakeLists.txt` for one outer `cmake --build` invocation.
   185: Each shared compiler tree builds Debug and Release through one cross-config
   186: Ninja process, so concurrent builds never write the same `.ninja_deps` or
   187: .ninja_log`. One shared CMake job pool admits the outer compiler and test
   188: commands, so a completed tree can release its slot to its tests while other
   189: trees continue compiling. On hosts with four or fewer logical CPUs, it admits
   190: one tree per CPU and sets every inner Ninja and `BUSTER_TEST_JOBS` quota to
   191: one; the six-tree Windows matrix therefore runs four one-job compiler trees
   192: at a time without nested oversubscription. Larger hosts retain the weighted
   193: allocator: split trees share at least two logical CPUs per admission slot while
   194: unity trees use one job. Clang tests then run concurrently in the same bounded
   195: pool, with each tree's quota passed through `BUSTER_TEST_JOBS`; future multithreaded test work
   196: must honor that limit. Application builds are multithreaded by default;

   217: consumes the producer's one-shot integrity-checked compiler/tool/cache/graph/
   218: environment provenance record before validating and snapshotting the artifact,
   219: runs the existing direct fixed-point workflow without starting an inner Ninja
   220: process, and remains disabled for the direct scheduler and unsupported platforms.
   221: Each self-host stage and the stage-2 benchmark are bounded at ten minutes
   222: (`SELF_HOST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`): the work is fixed and costs seconds, so a stage
   223: that does not finish is a compiler that never will, and waiting on one wedges
   224: a serialized CI runner for hours while Ninja buffers the edge's output and the
   225: log says nothing. On expiry the child is killed and the run fails naming the
   226: stage and its command line. Every other run waits indefinitely, because their
   227: cost scales with what they are given.
   228: The fixed-point pair continues to use the default FAST allocator, and the
   229: existing non-Windows machine stage continues to compile and run its benchmark
   230: with `-fregister-allocator=mir-stack`. That stage is followed by a canonical
   231: compile-only gate: the stage-2 compiler builds `ide-stage2-none` with
   232: `-fregister-allocator=none`. It does not run that output because the regression
   233: this gate protects against is a canonical argument-capture crash while

   239: CI Release builds use `-O2`; local Release builds retain the toolchain default.
   240: Local builds make the optimized tree profilable, which CMake's defaults do not:
   241: `BUSTER_DEBUG_INFO` emits debug information in the configurations that carry no
   242: `-g` (`Release`, `MinSizeRel`) and `BUSTER_FRAME_POINTERS` adds
   243: `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` to every optimized configuration. Both default to off
   244: under `--ci` and on everywhere else, and both are overridable with
   245: `./build.sh generate -DBUSTER_DEBUG_INFO=ON|OFF -DBUSTER_FRAME_POINTERS=ON|OFF`.
   246: `Debug` and `RelWithDebInfo` already carry `-g` from the CMake defaults, `Debug`
   247: is `-O0` and keeps frame pointers anyway, and sanitized trees keep their own
   248: reduced `-gline-tables-only` mode, so neither option disturbs them. MSVC is
   249: excluded from the frame-pointer option because `/Oy` has no x64 meaning.
   250: Measured on Clang 22/Linux x86-64: debug information does not change code
   251: generation and costs compile time and artifact size only (unity Release
   252: `ide.c` 37.3 s -> 46.5 s, `ide` 11.4 MiB -> 19.1 MiB); frame pointers do change
   253: code generation but cost 0.065% of instructions on a unity self-compile
   254: (29.5037 G -> 29.5227 G) with no wall-clock difference above run-to-run noise

   257: Clang static analysis runs only against unsanitized Release. The native driver

   262: configuration runs `test_all`; GCC, Zig, and MSVC are compile-only, and platform
   263: packages use their native test runner.
   264: The one carve-out inside `test_all` is a **whole-table audit**: a module whose
   265: result is a function of the generated metadata tables and the repository's
   266: source text alone, so no compiler, configuration or optimization level can
   267: change its answer. Those modules run on the same single canonical tree per
   268: platform that already owns `clang_analyze` — unsanitized optimized Clang —
   269: because re-deriving one identical answer in eight to ten configurations cost
   270: more than any other single thing in CI. Mark such a module with
   271: `table_audit` in the `test_descriptors` table of `src/buster/tests/test.c`;
   272: `x86_64_completion_census_tests` is the current one. The superbuild opts a
   273: tree out with `BUSTER_TEST_TABLE_AUDITS=0`, and **the default is on**, so a
   274: bare `ide test`, a single-tree build, or any runner that does not set the
   275: variable keeps full coverage. Never mark a module whose result depends on
   276: generated code, the host, or the sanitizer.
   277: Flag scope matters: `--sanitize`, `--fuzz`, `--lto`, `--ci`, `--time-trace`,
   278: `--instrument`, `--cc <clang|gcc|zig|cl>` are accepted **only by
   279: `generate`** for public workflows; `build` rejects them with an explicit
   280: diagnostic. The internal `self_host_from_existing` worker is the narrow
   281: exception for build-driver-supplied `--ci/--no-ci` and
   282: `--fuzz/--no-fuzz`, and requires the captured provenance record.
   283: 
   284: Sanitized correctness trees compile and link with
   285: `-fno-sanitize-recover=all`. Their generated test commands set fatal ASan and
   286: UBSan options, enable LeakSanitizer on native Linux Clang/GCC with a distinctive
   287: exit code, and print the effective policy during the registered suite.
   288: `ASAN_OPTIONS`, `UBSAN_OPTIONS`
   289: and `LSAN_OPTIONS` from the configuring shell are deliberately not copied into
   290: the build graph. Values exported only before an incremental `build` are also
   291: replaced by the generated command. This fixed precedence prevents
   292: `halt_on_error=0` or an old suppression path from turning a correctness gate
   293: into a diagnostic-only run. Invoke a built binary directly, outside the
   294: `test_all`/`test_ide` targets, for exploratory recovery behavior; that run is
   295: not a correctness result.
   296: 
   297: Generated test commands also set `BUSTER_SANITIZER_POLICY_MODE=fatal` or
   298: `unsupported`. The registered test treats missing fatal sanitizer options as a
   299: failure; child processes without the generated launcher marker remain quiet.
   300: 
   301: Headless tests never load an LSan suppression file. The Linux Vulkan loader's
   302: dynamic-library-unloading workaround is present only in configurations built
   303: with `BUSTER_USE_VULKAN=ON`; it is not a leak suppression and is absent from
   304: the default compiler configuration. Add no generic thread-entry or Buster
   305: application-frame suppression to a correctness target.
   306: 
   307: TCC is reserved for compiling `build.c` through `build.sh`/`build.ps1` and
   308: `generate --cc tcc` is rejected as an application compiler.
   309: `--optimize`/`--no-optimize` are configuration shorthands for
   310: Release/Debug and never create separate cached optimization state. `build`
   311: accepts `--config <name>`, `--optimize`, `--target/-t <ninja target>`, and
   312: `--verbose/-v`. Booleans have `--no-` twins; `--` passes the rest through to
   313: Ninja (`build`) or CMake (`generate`).

   325: ## Incremental Android test assets
   326: 
   327: The Android `apk` graph in `cmake/AndroidApk.cmake` treats the active files under
   328: `tests/` as package inputs, not compiler sources. After configuring the normal
   329: Android tree, `cmake --build build/android-ci-x86_64 --config Debug --target apk`
   330: repackages fixture edits, additions, renames and deletions without requiring a
   331: C source rebuild or another destructive `generate`. Release uses the same
   332: contract. An unchanged build does not repackage. A content-stable inventory
   333: handles removals and newly added files whose timestamps predate the APK;
   334: `CONFIGURE_DEPENDS` refreshes that inventory with the supported Ninja generators.
   335: The preserved `.bbb` corpus is excluded before Android asset packaging.
   336: 
   337: `python3 tests/android_apk_assets_test.py` exercises that same production graph
   338: through real CMake and Ninja Multi-Config, in Debug and Release, with isolated
   339: fixtures and controlled packaging-tool stand-ins. It checks package contents,
   340: fixture-only invalidation, stale-file removal, no-op behavior, and the retained
   341: native-library/manifest/sign-script dependencies. It requires the existing
   342: CMake, Ninja, Python and Bash prerequisites, not an Android SDK or a compiler.
   343: The existing `tests/mobile_ci_scripts_test.sh` suite and mobile lifecycle CI run
   344: it on Linux and macOS. This is build-graph evidence, not Android compilation,
   345: signing or device execution; those remain the regular Android mobile CI gates.
   346: Do not run two configurations' packaging concurrently in one build directory:
   347: the existing APK and staging paths are shared.

   349: ## Incremental iOS test assets
   350: 
   351: The iOS `ide` target stages active files under `tests/` through
   352: `cmake/IOSBundleAssets.cmake`. Its filtered, content-stable inventory makes
   353: fixture edits, additions, renames and removals update the configuration's app
   354: bundle without relinking the native executable. The owned `tests` subtree is
   355: rebuilt on a real input change, so deleted files cannot survive; preserved
   356: `.bbb` inputs are excluded and do not invalidate the graph. Debug and Release
   357: use separate stamps and bundles, and an unchanged build does not rewrite either.
